If 'oref.%IsA("Sample.Person") Return "Wrong class"

2.explanation: %ClassName with no argument returns the short name Invoice. Passing 1 returns the full name MyApp.Invoice. Choose the full name when package identity matters.

3.explanation: $CLASSMETHOD takes the class and method names, then forwards the remaining arguments. In this call the selected class is App.Plugins.EmailNotifier and the entry point is its Send class method.

4.explanation: $METHOD dispatches on the supplied object reference. The method name resolves to Add on that object, and its arguments are forwarded as supplied. The sum in the example is 30.

5.explanation: The string User.Person selects the class at runtime. $CLASSMETHOD invokes %New and returns its object reference. %ClassName(1) reads the full class name from that object.

6.explanation: $ISOBJECT distinguishes a valid OREF from an ordinary value. The first operand is not an object and gives 0. The created object gives 1. Test validity before invoking instance methods on uncertain input.

7.explanation: $PROPERTY reads the property whose name is in the variable. It therefore reads the same value as a direct access to the selected name property and returns Alice.

8.explanation: %Dictionary.ClassDefinition is keyed by the fully qualified class name. %OpenId("User.Person") retrieves its source definition object. A compiled dictionary class is a different view of the class after inheritance and compilation.

9.explanation: The loop enumerates the class definition's Properties collection and reads its entries. This is the declared view of User.Person. Use compiled property metadata when inherited properties are also relevant.

10.explanation: %ClassName(1) and $CLASSNAME give a full name, %IsA tests an object's class hierarchy, and $ISOBJECT tests reference validity. %Extends is a class-level inheritance query. Distinguish that query from inspecting the current object's actual type.

11.explanation: The three predicates succeed because the instance belongs to its own class and the tested ancestors. %IsA walks the hierarchy. A comparison of only the concrete class name would answer a narrower question.

12.explanation: Using $PROPERTY on the left side of SET writes the property selected by name. propName contains Timeout, so obj.Timeout is set to 30. The usual property behavior still applies.

13.explanation: CompiledMethod describes methods in the compiled class view, including inherited members that are available there. Use it to answer what can be called. Use MethodDefinition to inspect what was declared in the source.

14.explanation: A PropertyDefinition entry describes a declaration, including its name, type and keywords such as Required and SqlFieldName. These are metadata values. To read the value on a specific object, use its OREF and a property access.

15.explanation: The class and method strings identify App.EmailHandler.Process, and the remaining argument is passed unchanged. This is the same target as the direct class method call. In application code resolve external names through an allowed set.

1.explanation: A file character stream represents text in a filesystem file. It supports line-oriented reads, so the program can handle a large log without loading it into a single string. Use the binary counterpart for byte-preserving reads.

2.explanation: Bind the stream to the intended file, write the text and check the status of the operation. In production prefer the class's documented linking and open modes so you can control whether an existing file is replaced or appended to.

3.explanation: Loop until AtEnd and use ReadLine when the unit of work is a line. WRITE with an exclamation mark displays each returned line separately. For arbitrary binary data, use bounded Read calls instead.

4.explanation: Rewind moves the read cursor back to the beginning. It leaves the content in the stream intact, so a following Read starts again from the first chunk.

5.explanation: Call CopyFrom on the destination with the source stream as the argument. Check the returned status and confirm the source position when copying a partially consumed stream. Match character or binary types to the data.

6.explanation: The two Write calls contribute Hello and World in sequence, with the explicit space in the first chunk. Rewind resets the read position, so the following Read yields Hello World.

7.explanation: Choose two axes independently. File versus Global decides where the stream is backed, and Character versus Binary decides whether the API treats the content as text or bytes. That gives the four classes listed in the question.

8.explanation: Configure the request's server and transport, then call Get with the path. Check the returned %Status for transport errors. On success, inspect HttpResponse.StatusCode before interpreting the body.

example.title: Inspect transport and HTTP outcomes separately
example.code:
Set req = ##class(%Net.HttpRequest).%New()
Set req.Server = "api.example.com"
Set sc = req.Get("/data")
If $SYSTEM.Status.IsError(sc) {
    Do $SYSTEM.Status.DisplayError(sc)
    Quit
}
Write req.HttpResponse.StatusCode, !
example.note: The host is illustrative. Configure HTTPS and its TLS profile when the actual endpoint requires them.

9.explanation: HttpResponse.Data is a stream for the response body. Read from that stream in bounded chunks for a large payload. Check the HTTP status code first because an error response can also contain a body.

10.explanation: The request is a POST to /users. The JSON content is written to the request body and the content type tells the receiver how to interpret it. Check transport and HTTP status separately.

11.explanation: The request class has helpers for GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and PATCH. Choose the verb required by the endpoint. Each helper returns a transport status and exposes the server response through HttpResponse.

12.explanation: MailMessage holds recipients, subject and body. SMTP owns the transport and sends that message through the configured server. Keeping those roles separate lets you build the content before attempting the connection.

13.explanation: Populate the message object, add a recipient, write the body and pass the message to SMTP.Send. In ObjectScript invoke a body write with DO or capture its status. The quiz option shows the sequence, but the bare SET before the Write call must be corrected.

14.explanation: %Net.FtpSession is the FTP client API. Establish the session, choose the transfer mode that preserves your content, and check the result of each transfer. The FTP interface should not be confused with a different protocol such as SFTP.

15.explanation: Server and Port select the destination, Https enables TLS, ContentType sets the content-type header, and SetHeader can supply another header. For a real HTTPS request, also configure the required SSLConfiguration for the target.

1.explanation: The error is from the macro preprocessor, before the method runs. Confirm the include is visible to the class and actually defines the macro. A class-level Include states the dependency explicitly, but the error alone cannot distinguish a missing definition from an include that was not loaded.

2.explanation: The include file is present, but it defines LogInfo rather than LogError. The preprocessor looks for the exact macro name used by the call. Add the intended definition or correct the call, then recompile consumers.

3.explanation: Both samples come from the same numeric elapsed-time counter. Subtracting the earlier from the later value yields seconds, including fractions. This measures elapsed time within the current instance uptime.

example.title: Time just the operation under investigation
example.code:
Set start = $ZHOROLOG
Do ..ProcessBatch()
Write "Seconds: ", $ZHOROLOG-start, !

4.explanation: Both $HOROLOG samples contain a day count followed by seconds since midnight. Subtraction coerces them to their leading day numbers, so two samples on the same day give 0, not elapsed seconds. The exact 66818 shown in the question does not follow from those two same-day samples. Use two $ZHOROLOG samples for the benchmark.

5.explanation: Run the utility from a terminal in %SYS with appropriate permissions. Its counters describe instance activity over a sampling interval. Record the workload and interval so later comparisons have context.

6.explanation: The compiler is trying to resolve a property data type. %Strig does not name the standard string type. Correct it to %String, then recompile and check the first remaining compiler diagnostic.

7.explanation: The subclass depends on the compiled superclass. The presence of its source does not establish that compilation succeeded in this namespace. Compile App.Base.Record, fix its own errors if any, then compile the subclass.

8.explanation: Use SQL performance tools to relate a statement's plan to measured execution work. A plan shows the access path and joins. Runtime statistics tell you how much work that execution actually performed.

9.explanation: A small number of executions can pay cold preparation or cache costs while most reuse compiled logic. That pattern can raise P99 without affecting the median much. Measure preparation and execution separately to test the cache hypothesis.

10.explanation: RETURN is an ObjectScript command and its spelling is case-insensitive. Return, return and RETURN select the same command. Variable names in the same code still need their correct case.

11.explanation: The recursive compilation option can bring in dependency predecessors before compiling the supplied classes. Check the qualifiers supported by the target version and read the first dependency failure rather than just the final subclass error.

12.explanation: Both a missing macro definition and a malformed #If expression are errors in preprocessing. Reproduce by expanding the macro or checking the conditional directive. A runtime exception in the method would occur in a different phase.

13.explanation: Macro definitions are visible through the relevant compilation scope and includes. Defining DbName elsewhere in the project is insufficient unless this class's preprocessor can see it. The compile error names the unresolved macro.

14.explanation: Low global-buffer efficiency can indicate more database block reads per global reference. Verify the cause with physical read counters over the same interval. The ratio by itself does not distinguish a cold cache from a scan-heavy workload.

15.explanation: The line-by-line monitor attributes elapsed work and execution counts to specific routine lines. A line can dominate by running very often or by doing expensive work each time. Use both values when choosing what to inspect next.

1.explanation: Iterate through the stack levels and use $STACK(level,"PLACE") to get each execution location. Capture the stack while the relevant frames are still present, or use the exception's captured diagnostics after unwinding.

2.explanation: The catch variable is an exception object. AsStatus converts that object to the status representation expected by an API returning %Status. Keep the original exception if the caller also needs its location or other metadata.

3.explanation: If %OpenId fails to return an object, the following property access has no valid OREF and raises <INVALID OREF>. Check the open result and its status first to report the underlying lookup failure.

4.explanation: ThrowOnError bridges a status-returning API and exception handling. A success status lets the next line execute. An error status is wrapped in a status exception, so the nearest matching CATCH can handle it.

5.explanation: $STACK(-1) gives the current stack depth for iterating frame levels. It is not the text of a frame. Ask for a specific level and detail such as PLACE when you want diagnostic output.

6.explanation: THROW accepts an exception object, such as %Exception.General created with a name and details. A status-throwing macro wraps a failing %Status in an exception. The catch block can inspect the object or convert it back to status.

7.explanation: StatusException represents an existing %Status within exception handling. General lets application code create a named exception with its own details. Choose based on whether you are propagating an existing status or creating a new exception.

8.explanation: GetErrorText formats the status into readable text for a human. Preserve the original status for programmatic checks or propagation. The formatted text is useful for logs and display.

9.explanation: Use $$$ISOK(sc) to test success and $$$ISERR(sc) to test failure. Keep that check separate from interpreting the returned data. A status is not itself the domain value or SQLCODE.

10.explanation: THROW ex propagates the exception caught by the current handler. You can log it before rethrowing and let an outer handler choose the policy. Replacing it with a new exception would change the diagnostic context.

11.explanation: One option throws through the status macro, and the other explicitly creates a StatusException from the error status before throwing it. Both carry the original status through the catch boundary.

12.explanation: ProcessOrder names the label, +7 is its routine offset and App.OrderService.1 is the generated routine. Use the class and method source to map the offset before guessing which expression failed.

13.explanation: Name describes the error kind, Code carries a numeric error code and Location identifies where it occurred. These properties capture distinct parts of the diagnostic. Log all relevant fields rather than encoding the whole exception as just a name.

14.explanation: $$$ADDSC combines the accumulated status and a new error into one compound status. This is useful when independent steps each need validation. It preserves more information than overwriting sc after every check.

15.explanation: DecomposeStatus exposes the individual errors inside a compound status through its output array. Use it to present or log the failures separately instead of treating the combined status as one opaque string.

16.explanation: Step1 returns a value, so execution continues in the caller until the code explicitly returns or throws. The shown error branch returns the same status. The CATCH runs only if something throws an exception.

example.title: Convert a returned status only if exception flow is intended

17.explanation: $STACK(-1) reports the depth. For a frame with available source, $STACK(level,"MCODE") retrieves its code line. PLACE gives the execution location when source text is unavailable or you need a stable location.

18.explanation: The routine stores a formatted error entry and then records information for each frame it iterates. That is the stack observed by the logging code. Preserve exception location separately when you need the original failure frame after unwinding.

1.explanation: Namespace access depends on the resources of its mapped databases. The job can run in one namespace and still lack access to a database it references after switching. Check the job's identity and the destination database resource.

2.explanation: The error names ordKey because the code evaluates it before it has been assigned. If key was meant to be the $ORDER cursor, use that name consistently and initialize it before the first traversal step.

3.explanation: $ORDER returns the empty sentinel at the end. Moving the QUIT below WRITE lets the code use that sentinel as an array subscript first. Move the exit check immediately after $ORDER. The exact error depends on what kind of array or global is accessed.

example.title: Stop before reading the end-of-traversal sentinel
example.note: For an array with branch-only nodes, check for a value before the final read.

4.explanation: Each recursive call needs a smaller argument and a base case that returns without recursing. With the base case for n <= 1, Factorial(5) eventually reaches 1 and the calls can unwind instead of exhausting the stack.

5.explanation: The expression refers to agee but the prior assignment defines age. Since those are different names, concatenation attempts to read an undefined variable. Correct the identifier where it is read.

6.explanation: The error identifies config as the undefined value and gives a location relative to the zProcess label in App.Engine.1. Find the corresponding source line and trace where config should have been assigned on that path.

7.explanation: A write can fail because the database is mounted read-only or because the process lacks permission on the relevant database resource. Verify the actual mapped database and the permissions of the failing process, including a background job's identity.

8.explanation: $GET(timeout,default) reads the variable if it has a value and returns the fallback otherwise. It avoids an undefined-variable error. An explicitly set empty string is still an assigned value.

9.explanation: Position 3 exists but has no defined element because the constructor skipped that argument. Direct $LIST access raises <NULL VALUE>. If the position is optional, use $LISTGET with a fallback or check its presence before reading.

10.explanation: The loop expands the key until it exceeds the encoded subscript limit. At that point the global reference is invalid and raises <SUBSCRIPT>. Store long data as a node value and use a bounded key.

11.explanation: An invalid global subscript or an oversized encoded key can raise <SUBSCRIPT>. The empty global subscript case depends on configuration and context. Test the exact global reference in the target environment rather than assuming that every empty subscript is forbidden.

12.explanation: The destination here is the protected system database, so the application user cannot write under the stated permissions. Confirm the actual mapping and database resource before changing code or asking for broader access.

13.explanation: The first addition reads total before any assignment. Initialize it to 0 before the loop so every path has a defined accumulator, including the empty input case.

14.explanation: ObjectScript local variable names are case-sensitive. The query assigns city but the SET uses City as a subscript. Use the variable actually populated by the query.

15.explanation: <SUBSCRIPT> points to a bad key or subscript for the accessed node. <FRAMESTACK> points to exhausting stack space, for example through unbounded recursion. Inspect the referenced key for the former and the repeated call path for the latter.

16.explanation: With no variadic arguments, the count node may be absent. Use $GET(scores,0) for the count and decide what an average of zero inputs should return before doing division.

17.explanation: Every visited node still has a Next value, so the loop never reaches its exit condition. An iterative cycle does not increase recursion depth. Track visited IDs or impose a valid termination condition to detect the cycle.

18.explanation: After the record is deleted, the open can return an empty value. Reading .Email on that value raises <INVALID OREF>. Check the open outcome before reading the property and handle deletion as a lookup failure.
